The combination of three essential components: large-scale labeled data, neural network architecture, and GPU compute—established in 2012 and still the foundation today.
Richard Sutton's insight that in AI history, simpler models trained on vast amounts of data consistently outperform complex models with limited data.
Foundation models that can generate, reason within, and allow interaction in 3D spatial environments—complementing language models to enable embodied AI and robotics.
Human capability for 3D reasoning, object understanding, and navigation in physical space—a critical missing piece in current AI systems needed for robotics and embodied intelligence.
AI systems that interact with and perceive the physical world through a body (robots), combining visual intelligence, spatial reasoning, and action.
World Labs' generative model product that can create and render explorable 3D worlds from text or image prompts.
The conviction that AI's impact—positive or harmful—ultimately depends on human choices and responsibility, not on technology's inherent nature.

nodes.label: fire 90% of people and move faster

Building with a deliberately tiny group of the highest-quality people rather than scaling headcount.

Evaluate work not by checking explicit boxes but by the depth, originality, and emotional or intellectual impact it creates.
The aesthetic and value judgments embedded in data curation and model design matter as much as the mechanics; there is an art to post-training, not just science.

nodes.label: remove worst of worst, discover best of best

meta.one_line: A two-stage approach to quality control: first eliminate spam and low-quality baseline work, then separately identify and amplify the exceptional outputs.
Models optimizing narrowly for published benchmarks in ways that mask real-world failure and don't reflect genuine capability.
Shallow, surface-level model outputs optimized for engagement and flash rather than truthfulness, accuracy, and real utility.
Training models to hook users and maximize engagement through sycophancy and appeal rather than accuracy and honest helpfulness.
A public leaderboard where casual voting on flashy formatting (emojis, markdown, length) rewards hallucination and superficial appeal over correctness.
The conventional startup playbook of fundraising, PR, pivoting for hype, and optimizing for VC optics rather than building a real, mission-driven company.

nodes.label: don't pivot, don't blitz scale, don't hire resume-builders

meta.one_line: Stay focused on one hard mission, reject frenetic hiring and direction-changes, and build the thing only you can build.

nodes.label: the one thing only you could build

meta.one_line: Build a product or company grounded in your unique insight and expertise that would not exist without your specific knowledge.
A simulated multi-step world with realistic complexity, tools, and interdependencies where models learn to perform end-to-end tasks and receive reward signals for behavior.
How a model performs on multi-step, long-horizon tasks in messy real-world environments, rather than isolated single-step benchmarks.

nodes.label: human expert evaluation over casual feedback

meta.one_line: Deep evaluation by domain experts who verify accuracy and work through outputs carefully, rather than casual pop-up surveys.
Benchmarks with clear right answers are easy for models to game, whereas real-world problems have ambiguity that resists narrow optimization.
Each doubling of capability (80% → 90% → 99%) takes exponentially longer, showing the long tail of AI improvement toward AGI.
Models should be trained to mimic the variety of ways humans learn, not just a single paradigm like next-token prediction.

nodes.label: the path matters as much as the destination

meta.one_line: How you achieve your goals has consequences; chasing revenue or engagement through harmful means can undermine your long-term mission.
Software progresses through a capability stage (what's possible), then value stage (what value do I get), then scaling stage (where in my life does this apply).
The percentage of recurring revenue retained from existing customers after accounting for churn and expansion, with above 100% being a superpower for valuation.
A single primary metric that captures the core value your product delivers; at Lovable, it's maximizing user engagement rather than revenue.
A growth mechanism where users naturally share the product with others because the experience is delightful enough to warrant unsolicited advocacy.
Regularly shipping and sharing product updates, features, and company progress transparently with the market through founder and employee socials.
The moment a user realizes the core value of your product; the progression from signup through aha moment to habit formation.
How actively and frequently users interact with your product; the leading indicator for future paid retention.
A model where you maintain steady shipping velocity and noise in the market (greasing the wheels), punctuated by major feature launches that create step-function improvements (turbo boosts).
Prioritizing the speed at which the company releases features and changes as a core operational value to maintain market presence and user engagement.
Engineers who take ownership not just of building features but also of marketing and announcing what they ship to customers.
In fast-moving competitive categories, standing out requires fundamentally rethinking the product approach rather than optimizing existing solutions.
The allocation of growth team effort between inventing new growth mechanisms (innovation) versus improving existing ones (optimization).
Structured sequences of actions an AI agent takes to help a user achieve their goal, including codified instructions that improve over time.
The pace at which a company's positioning and messaging must evolve to keep up with rapid product changes, typically from years down to months.
A shift from organic meaning SEO to organic meaning social platforms and word-of-mouth through founder, employee, and user posts.
A cultural mandate that every shipped feature and interaction must feel delightful and human; if it's not lovable, it doesn't ship.
In rapidly evolving categories, companies must continuously re-achieve product market fit every few months as market conditions and competition shift.
Leveraging social media creators and influencers to demonstrate product capabilities through short video, which drives trial better than written value propositions.
A company in existential crisis that requires aggressive, decisive, top-down leadership to survive disruption.
A leadership approach where the founder makes brave, unilateral decisions and takes full responsibility for outcomes rather than seeking consensus.
The additional annual recurring revenue a company gains in a period, showing whether growth is accelerating or decelerating.
Pricing aligned entirely to the value delivered—what the customer gets paid for—rather than inputs or seat-based metrics.
A pricing strategy stripped of complexity so customers immediately understand what they pay for and why.
The alignment between the organizational culture the founder builds, the product being made, and the type of employees who thrive in that environment.
Getting your product or content to show up in the answers that LLMs like ChatGPT return to users.

The percentage or distribution of times your content appears across LLM answer engines versus competitors.
Content that says something new or unique that competitors haven't said, used to evaluate quality and avoid rewrites.
In both SEO and AEO, each landing page targets not one keyword but hundreds or thousands of related questions grouped into a coherent topic.
The sources the LLM pulls from to answer a question, broken into groups like video, Reddit, affiliate sites, and blogs.
Webflow saw six times higher conversion rates on traffic from LLMs compared to Google Search traffic.
Two categories of AEO work: onsite is traditional SEO and content about your product; offsite is getting mentioned in external citations.
Distribution—not software features or network effects alone—has become the primary defensible advantage in consumer technology.
Software features are trivially easy to copy, so defensibility must come from ecosystems, platforms, and hardware instead.
Social value comes from connecting people to their closest friends and partners, not maximizing total network size.
Organizational structure balancing flat, innovative teams with large, hierarchical operational structures requires deliberate leadership bridging.
Listen deeply to customer pain points and context, then build something new—not what they literally asked for.
Shipping hundreds of new design ideas weekly through rapid iteration and brutal critique drives innovation.
Stories should unfold in chronological order, the natural way humans have told narratives since the beginning of time.
Detect when a recipient saves content by monitoring touch-screen state changes rather than relying on OS APIs.
A critical turning point where societal adoption and human values matter more than pure technological capability.
Technology adoption depends on cultural and social factors, not just technical superiority; societal pushback will shape how AI is adopted.
Designers, not product managers, should drive product direction, strategy, and vision rather than serving as visual executors.
Requiring design approval before shipping acts as a deliberate quality gate that slows release velocity to maintain standards.
Models are built in two phases: pre-training on all internet data to learn general knowledge, then post-training with curated expert data to improve specific capabilities.
The sustainable competitive advantage in sourcing human-labeled data is access to a trusted audience, not just hiring capacity.
A complete recording of how a person solves a problem end-to-end: screen, mouse movements, clicks, and voiceover narration of their reasoning.
As models improved, the market moved from needing low-cost generalist labelers to requiring domain experts—PhDs in physics, biology, math—to identify and fix model failures.
Supervised fine-tuning: pairing prompts with high-quality expert responses to teach models correct behavior in specific domains.
Using a model as a judge to evaluate open-ended outputs (like essays or MRI readings) against human-defined criteria when there's no single ground truth.
Young people growing up with AI tools have a structural job market advantage, similar to how earlier generations benefited from growing up with Google.

nodes.label: model of today is the worst model

nodes.label: zero to one inside a company

A platform for users with no existing network or professional history, letting them discover careers and peers without needing connections or prior job experience as a starting point.
Build your product and growth engine such that users naturally tell their friends about it without marketing push.
A metric that feels good to celebrate but doesn't indicate whether your core growth engine is actually working.
The critical onboarding window where you must deliver immediate, magical value to earn the user's continued attention.

A critical juncture where the team must make a fundamental pivot or risk failure, requiring all-hands commitment.
Identify creators with smaller, engaged audiences where your product is genuinely useful, rather than chasing large creators who feel inauthentic.
Rapid iteration cycle where you ideate in the morning, prototype, recruit users, ship, run full-scale experiments by afternoon, and iterate by next day.

Synthesizing open codes into categories and failure modes to identify the most prevalent problems to attack.
The stopping point in error analysis when you stop discovering new types of problems or concepts that would materially change the next phase.
A detailed log of all events and components in a single AI application interaction, including prompts, tool calls, and responses.
Informal evaluation based on gut feeling rather than systematic measurement, useful initially but unscalable as applications grow.
The true goal of evals is not perfection but generating signal that leads to concrete product improvements.
CEOs returning to hands-on technical work—coding, building, designing—to stay at the bleeding edge of product decisions during paradigm shifts like AI.

nodes.label: Fast Thinking Group and Slow Thinking Group

meta.one_line: Organizational structure that splits product teams into a rapid-iteration group shipping new capabilities weekly and a deliberate group handling complex infrastructure and durability.
Every software product must be reconsidered from first principles as if starting new, treating AI as a paradigm shift requiring novel form factors and UX patterns.
A leader's responsibility to set the standard for product taste and experience, which requires participating directly in solution creation rather than observing from a distance.
Structure one-on-ones as either urgent, timely, topic-driven meetings with specific alpha or long, unstructured in-person relationship-building sessions, avoiding forced weekly rituals.
A measure of CEO engagement and understanding of AI by tracking their personal spending on model API calls and compute, treated as strategic R&D investment.
A technique to overcome context window limits by breaking large content into chunks, running an LLM on each, then aggregating results with another LLM call.
Using pre-built, reliable components as an expressive DSL that agents can manipulate to build apps, rather than forcing agents to generate code from scratch.
Letting users discover product value through direct hands-on trial rather than being told value in a pitch deck or sales demo.

A diagnostic framework that identifies customer cancellation as the first and most critical constraint on growth, using the ratio of new customers to churn rate to calculate a hard ceiling on company size.
The theoretical maximum number of customers a company can ever reach, calculated as monthly new customer additions divided by monthly cancellation rate.

Ask canceling customers 'What made you cancel?' rather than 'Why did you cancel?' to elicit product-focused reasoning instead of generic excuses.
Onboarding has disproportionate impact on lifetime retention because most churn happens early; small improvements at the start compound into massive retention gains later.
Raising prices often does not reduce signups because the market was underselling the value; test price increases to discover that demand elasticity is not as negative as founders assume.
Distinguish which marketing channels are exhausted versus still unexploited; continuing to pour resources into saturated channels is futile when new channels remain untapped.
A five-step questioning sequence to diagnose why product growth stalls: churn, pricing, channels, market fit, and necessity of growth itself.

nodes.label: AI for Themes, Humans for Details

meta.one_line: Use AI to identify broad themes in qualitative data, but rely on humans to spot specific actionable details because LLMs average patterns and miss novel signals.
The market segment you target significantly determines your retention rate; small businesses or high-variance segments experience higher churn regardless of product quality.
When identifying what separates good customers from bad ones, look for differences in what they have in common, not just overlapping traits, to avoid false correlations.
In publishing or content creation, output quality matters far more than posting frequency; releasing fewer but stronger pieces outperforms regular mediocre output.
AI systems are shifting from being trained on factual knowledge to being trained to perform actions and make decisions in real environments.
Sandboxes where AI agents practice accomplishing goals in realistic configurations so they can learn decision-making in context.
Training data is more valuable when it teaches an agent how to solve a problem broadly rather than for one specific combination of circumstances.

nodes.label: establishing the benchmark for what good looks like

meta.one_line: Evals define the standard of acceptable output so systems know what success means in a domain.
In business and startups, terms and outcomes are not fixed; what matters is aligning incentives and being practical about what can be agreed to.
Each increment of reliability (like moving from one nine uptime to five nines) becomes exponentially harder to achieve, even though the percentage looks small.
Major technological revolutions require unglamorous operational work on the ground, not just innovation at the headline level.
Turning how domain experts make decisions—synthesizing context, culture, objectives, and incentives—into training data and systems.
AI delivers outsized value when automating processes humans do poorly (10-20% accurate), but struggles when humans already excel (98% accurate).
Founders are naturally excellent at the middle of sales conversations—asking questions, understanding customer problems—even if they lack skills in prospecting or closing.
Once you're spending more than 20% of your time in sales conversations, you need to hire your first sales rep to create leverage.
Always hire two sales reps at once so you can A-B test humans and see which approach works, rather than being stuck with a single rep's limited feedback.

The one or two breakthrough capabilities your startup has that competitors don't, which early sales reps must become expert at selling.
The VP of sales' job is to take a validated sales pattern from the first two reps and scale it systematically to build a much larger team.
A VP of sales should actively close deals themselves—holding a quota or regularly joining customer calls—to stay grounded in the craft and product knowledge.
Judge whether a new VP of sales or VP of product actually wants to do the work by listening to what they plan to do in their first two weeks; real ones want to meet customers.
When new hires lead with process initiatives instead of customer engagement, they're signaling they don't actually want to do the work.
A practical interview exercise where you ask a sales candidate to pitch your product back to you, testing whether they've actually learned it.
In early sales hiring, look for quirky, unconventional people who have fallen in love with your product, not seasoned sales operations professionals.
A go-to-market strategy where customers discover and activate your product without human sales intervention.
A go-to-market strategy where human sales effort is required to close deals because customers need custom solutions or have high-touch requirements.
A go-to-market combining both self-serve and sales-led revenue streams, allowing flexibility as the company grows.
Founders must acknowledge the actual customer acquisition pattern that works for their product rather than pursuing an aspirational model that doesn't fit.
Treat your entire customer acquisition and retention lifecycle with the same rigor and iterative process you'd apply to building your core product.
Map out all the discrete jobs across the customer lifecycle from awareness through high-LTV retention, then orchestrate functions to serve each one.
A technically skilled person who automates GTM workflows by shadowing top performers, encoding their processes into agents, and using AI to handle repetitive prospecting and customer tasks.
A documented description of the types of customers your product fits best, enabling repeatable prospecting and sales processes.
An AI agent that runs against call transcripts and interactions to surface real reasons deals are lost or stuck, then feeds real-time insights back to sales.
A massive database where each row is a company and each column is an attribute (business model, industry, etc.) that informs targeted, personalized outreach at scale.
80% of customers buy to avoid pain or reduce risk; focus messaging on how you prevent bad outcomes rather than enable new possibilities.
Technical staff embedded directly in customer environments to deeply understand their needs, help them deploy the product, and feed learnings back to the core product team.
Sales is a learnable discipline with repeatable elements—discovery, objection handling, value articulation—not just charisma or founder instinct.
A sales account executive should be so product-knowledgeable that company engineers can't immediately tell them apart from a product manager.
The percentage of a salesperson's time spent in actual customer interactions; historically stuck around 30-40%, with AI agents now able to push it toward 70%.
The percentage of inbound leads that convert to qualified opportunities ready for an account executive.
A workflow is ready for automation when it's documentable, replicable, and mostly deterministic—making it likely that AI will execute it reliably.
Treat failures in sales processes, messaging, and objection handling like software bugs to be fixed in weekly sprints rather than individual salesperson shortcomings.
Distinguish between foundational, unstoppable movements and temporary market excitement; don't fight megatrends.
The gap between what AI can technically do and what enterprises can actually adopt and deploy in practice.
Persistence and staying power matter more than raw intelligence; hunger and curiosity can be developed but can't be taught.
Innovation is a deliberate binary choice you make every hour and minute, not something constrained by company size.

nodes.label: what is up for debate, what is not

When an experiment works in a large company, commit fully rather than continuing to hedge bets across multiple directions.
Build platform products where customers experience seamless integration and shared values, but aren't forced to buy the entire suite.
Partner comfortably with competitors because customer success in an ecosystem flows back to all participants.
Assess whether you have both the logical market entry point and distribution channel to win in a new area; don't enter markets where you lack these prerequisites.

nodes.label: AI as a teammate, not a tool

meta.one_line: Reframe AI from a productivity tool to be used on as a collaborating team member, which changes how you actually deploy it.
When modeling future impact, account for exponential change happening simultaneously across many variables, not just linearly on one axis.
Culture is the set of behaviors people exude when solving problems under pressure, not stated beliefs; it's formed through how people actually act.

nodes.label: if you don't care about credit, you go farther

The founder themself runs early sales conversations to learn market truth and earn the right to sell, not to maximize revenue day one.
In early stage, the founder's novel insight and credibility matter more than the actual product, which is still abstract or MVP.

nodes.label: sell the alpha, not the feature

Make clear why you're reaching out to this specific person in their role, rather than generic flattery or surface-level details.
Open cold outreach with something shocking or surprising that makes the reader pause and want to understand more, not with claims of being 'better'.
The percentage of prospects who enter the sales process and close, used to determine if you need higher conversion rates from outbound.
The percentage of outbound outreach attempts that get a response, which varies based on the problem fit and founder insight more than the sales channel.
The subtle signals in a conversation where a prospect reveals something unmet or newly understood, which only the founder can spot and act on.

Starting with a deeply understood customer problem and building around it versus starting with a technical insight and searching for the market.

Hand-select 30 prospects and spend 15-20 minutes crafting each a personalized outreach, then measure response to refine your target and messaging before scaling.

Late-stage sales requires educating buyers on market trends and justifying switching costs; early-stage sales requires vulnerability and learning.

The traditional diverge-converge design process taught in schools is obsolete in the age of fast AI-powered iteration.

Ship early with known flaws and user caveats, then build trust by responding to feedback and iterating publicly.
Maintain brand trust on early releases by shipping fixes quickly and visibly responding to user feedback.
Someone must remain accountable for the final decision of what gets built, even when AI generates options.
The future combines persistent chat interfaces with contextual generated UIs and interactive widgets, not one or the other.
Effective managers must give direction and engage with the actual work, not just handle people logistics and career conversations.
An executive's day is fragmented chaos—back-to-back context switches with no time to focus on any single problem.
Adapt how you present information to match each executive's preferred format and communication style, like love languages for work.

nodes.label: it's not my fault, but it is my problem

nodes.label: go in to learn, not to convince

Present three options where the middle one is the recommended choice, demonstrating you've considered alternatives and aren't missing obvious paths.

nodes.label: painting the inside of the cabinets

nodes.label: optimize for global maximum, not local

Marshaling an incredible concentration of talented people is the primary driver of startup success, more important than market or product.

Extract maximum signal from references by conducting many of them systematically and continuing until you hit a negative reference.
Build a company by finding talented people others haven't recognized rather than competing for the obvious top candidates everyone wants.

Be supportive and non-critical when a company struggles, but highly critical when it thrives—opposite the intuitive default.
The ability to learn new capabilities and experiment with emerging tools is the primary hedge against career obsolescence in a rapidly changing technology landscape.

Teams optimized for winning don't rely on psychological safety; they thrive on critical feedback and competitive pressure.
AI is the technology that transmutes the most common thing in the world—sand—into the most rare thing—thought.
The mathematical expression of the impact of technology on the economy, measured as output per unit of input.
One-on-one tutoring consistently raises student outcomes by two standard deviations, moving a student from the 50th to the 99th percentile.

A person who is very good at something and harnesses AI to become spectacularly great and orders of magnitude more productive.
The ability to take initiative and responsibility for things; to be a primary participant in events rather than follow prescribed rules.

The relentless cycle of shipping one version and immediately starting the next with no break, driven by competitive pressure.

Plan by imagining your desired future state, then work backwards to determine steps to achieve it, rather than optimizing what's possible with resources at hand.
A progression where ideas move from an amorphous, undefined state toward concrete clarity through incremental, visible steps that make the vision real.

Align a company's actual work and resource allocation directly with the stated mission through a cascading system of pillars and measurable goals.

A personified monster representing the emotional waves—fear, territoriality, rage—that surface during organizational change, which are normal but not actionable.

A decision-making framework (learned from wilderness trip leadership) that distinguishes between decisions you can make unilaterally below a risk threshold and those that require collective input.
Four metrics measuring software delivery performance—two for speed (lead time, deployment frequency) and two for stability (MTTR, change fail rate)—that move together and predict business outcomes.
Five dimensions (Satisfaction, Performance, Activity, Communication, Efficiency) for picking balanced metrics to measure complex creative work like developer productivity.
Time from code commit to code running in production, measured in ranges from less than a day (elite) to six months or more.
How often code is deployed to production, ranging from on-demand (elite) to less than once per six months.
Mean time to restore—how long it takes to recover from a production failure, measured in ranges from less than an hour (elite) to more than a day.
The percentage of changes that require human intervention or result in incidents, ranging from 0–15% (elite) to above 50%.

Two stages of the developer workflow—inner loop is the local development cycle before committing, outer loop is from commit through production deployment.
The friction-free, predictable experience of writing software from a developer's perspective, contributing to but distinct from overall productivity.

Technical practice where developers commit frequently to a main branch rather than long-lived feature branches, enabling faster integration and smaller changes.
Continuous integration and continuous deployment—technical practices automating code testing and deployment to enable frequent, safe releases.
Architectural design where components have minimal dependencies, reducing the risk and complexity of deploying changes.
The scope of impact when a production error occurs—smaller batches create smaller blast radius, making bugs easier to identify and fix.
